sourceNote: Based on 243 simulated protocol 3.1 grid profiles, with 81 at each life-stage, standing, cushion, outlook and adaptability level. These are scenarios, not survey responses or population estimates.
overview: Across **243 simulated construction-worker profiles**, most keep paid site work in AI Plateau; AI changes plans and orders before robots handle physical building tasks.
**Household reserves** shape worry in every picture, even when similar local jobs are plentiful; a posted role still needs safe duties and sufficient pay.
**AGI by 2028** brings the highest average worry, while longer runways support savings, funded training and conditional job applications without guaranteeing work.

S0.headline: In AI Plateau, most construction workers keep building, while current bills and savings still divide their sense of security.

whatTheyDo.text: 234 of 243 profiles keep working; Aisha Zhang keeps taking day-rate kitchen and staircase jobs on new builds.
92 of 243 profiles make new savings or debt payments; Jamal Okafor moves a small amount from each pay packet into a shared emergency account.
66 of 243 profiles learn or test AI controls; Sam Weber tests the AI count checker on the next supply order.
36 of 243 profiles take collective action; Maya Novak asks her union branch to agree rules for site app data.
27 of 243 profiles cut spending; Rosa Torres stops buying lunch on site and saves that money for rent.

whatTheySay: **Physical fitting** still needs a person to measure openings, hang doors and notice where real walls differ from plans.
**Small office gains** may ease lists and forms, but most workers do not expect a new building process.
whatTheyThink: **Household money** needs watching in 73 profiles; 42 worry about the next contract, while one fears existing factory robots.
**Steadier work and income** feature in 107 profiles; 20 focus on strengthening trade skills.
howTheyFeel: **Calm** leads at 136 of 243 profiles; physical site work and paid hours remain broadly familiar.
Another **68 of 243** are anxious about existing bills or unreliable shifts even though AI changes little.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.77 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.00 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Learning AI is tagged for 38 of 81 adaptive profiles, versus 1 of 81 resistant profiles.
Average worry is 1.86 among 81 late-stage profiles, versus 1.53 among 81 early-stage profiles.

S1.headline: In Steady Disruption, construction workers protect paid site time while learning new planning tools and checking how office changes reach the crew.

whatTheyDo.text: 161 of 243 profiles keep working; Felix Rahman keeps taking paid framing shifts on his current building site.
156 of 243 profiles learn or test AI controls; Sam Weber learns the schedule system used to coordinate his crew.
80 of 243 profiles seek different paid work; Hassan Diaz applies to the council road crew for winter gritting work.
74 of 243 profiles take collective action; Rosa Ziegler collects actual crew hours with a steward and requests fair targets.
44 of 243 profiles cut spending; Pedro Baker postpones replacing the sofa if crew bonus payments fall.

whatTheySay: **Plans and buying** change before carpenters, roofers and other site workers lose the physical fitting work.
**Real measurements** and worker review still matter when faster software sets orders, schedules or targets.
whatTheyThink: **Site wages or hours** could shrink in 136 private-thought accounts, despite continuing hands-on work.
**Planning pressure**, household earners and shrinking thinking roles create distinct worries; 14 profiles see a potential upside.
howTheyFeel: **Anxiety** leads at 144 of 243 profiles as faster planning may affect paid hours, targets and household bills.
Only **15 of 243** are calm; most expect some pressure or disruption even while hands-on work continues.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.81 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 2.28 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Learning AI is tagged for 73 adaptive and 77 steady profiles, versus 6 resistant profiles (81 per group).
Seeking a different job is tagged for 45 of 81 late-stage profiles, versus 8 of 81 early-stage profiles.
Collective action is tagged for 70 progressive profiles, versus 2 centre and 2 traditional profiles (81 each).

S2.headline: In AGI by 2028, construction workers face immediate plan changes and a possible 2031 robot threat to paid hands-on work.

whatTheyDo.text: 177 of 243 profiles seek different paid work; Vera Lopez applies after 2028 only to posted local site-checking work with bill-covering pay and a paid course.
130 of 243 profiles keep working; Nikhil Abbott keeps paid fitting shifts and requests a written robot timetable.
108 of 243 profiles pursue practical or recognized training; David Petrov enrols in funded equipment maintenance training only if placements and practical hours exist.
74 of 243 profiles make new savings or debt payments; Vera Walsh overpays the mortgage by five hundred a month.
64 of 243 profiles cut spending; Chloe Abbott cancels the summer holiday and stops takeaways.

whatTheySay: **Planning and buying** could change by 2028, while capable hands-on robots follow around 2031.
Workers ask for **real safety trials** and a say in the timetable before builders cut paid site roles.
whatTheyThink: **Late-career wages** remain necessary in 61 profiles; 78 question how long savings or nearby jobs could replace lost pay.
**Planning and lead work** could change before robots arrive; 27 profiles also worry about another household income.
howTheyFeel: All **243 profiles** are anxious or alarmed about the fast transition and possible 2031 site robots.
The **70 alarmed** expect a major income blow; 173 anxious profiles still see some room to respond.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.49 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 3.07 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Retraining is tagged for 54 of 81 adaptive profiles, versus 16 of 81 resistant profiles.
A job change is tagged for 73 of 81 high-standing profiles, versus 47 of 81 low-standing profiles.
A job change is tagged for 76 of 81 late-stage profiles, versus 36 of 81 early-stage profiles.

quotes.text: Our three months of savings would run out long before the mortgage does.

quotes.name: Ben Khan

S3.headline: In AGI by 2031, the extra years shift many construction workers toward conditional training, job searches and continued paid site work.

whatTheyDo.text: 156 of 243 profiles pursue practical or recognized training; Zane Kowalski enrols in a building-services course if fees and paid release are agreed.
155 of 243 profiles seek different paid work; Vera Lopez applies after 2031 for a posted local quality role only if trained and the pay covers bills.
132 of 243 profiles keep working; Wei Evans keeps main paid framing shifts during a supervised retrofit trial.
93 of 243 profiles make new savings or debt payments; Rosa Larsen puts twenty a week into a separate account.
67 of 243 profiles learn or test AI controls; Jamal Okafor learns the contractor’s new site planning system on active jobs.

whatTheySay: **Five years** before thinking AI and roughly three more before capable building robots make preparation more practical.
Workers still want **paid training** and proof that new jobs cover the bills before leaving site wages.
whatTheyThink: **Retirement timing** cannot follow the robot calendar alone in 74 profiles; actual household figures still matter.
**Real paid roles** matter to 37 profiles; 36 see time to build skills or find more durable work.
howTheyFeel: Most remain **anxious** at 171 of 243, but 66 are uneasy and five are alarmed.
The **five alarmed** profiles are all early-stage, thin-cushion and resistant despite the longer warning.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.01 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 2.47 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Learning AI is tagged for 35 of 81 adaptive profiles, versus 3 of 81 resistant profiles.
Retraining is tagged for 66 of 81 mid-stage profiles, versus 43 of 81 late-stage profiles.

quotes.text: Five years feels like enough time to become better at repairs, but only if the training happens on paid hours while the mortgage is running.

S4.headline: In AGI by 2036, a decade lets many construction workers keep earning and build reserves, though thin cushions still limit choice.

whatTheyDo.text: 187 of 243 profiles keep working; Sam Haddad keeps kitchen-fitting shifts on the current site.
135 of 243 profiles make new savings or debt payments; Kira Wagner makes extra mortgage payments from overtime while preserving eleven months of savings.
104 of 243 profiles seek different paid work; Iris Abbott applies by 2039 only to posted local building roles whose pay covers household bills.
74 of 243 profiles pursue practical or recognized training; David Torres completes a funded assessor course only if an adequate local trainer post exists.
50 of 243 profiles take collective action; Elena Moreau presses the union safety committee for public-gate robot standards.

whatTheySay: **Ten years** before thinking AI and until around 2039 before capable robots gives builders room to plan.
Workers still insist on **site measurements**, safe trials and real wages behind any promised new role.
whatTheyThink: **Retirement finances or capacity** remain decisive in 81 profiles, even with a decade before thinking AI.
**Reliable wages** remain necessary in 46 accounts; 37 see time, savings or nearby options for choosing what comes next.
howTheyFeel: **Anxiety** remains in 92 of 243 profiles, often tied to household costs and uncertain future paid work.
Another **56 of 243** are calm and 95 uneasy; extra time helps, though it cannot guarantee work.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.79 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.56 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Learning AI is tagged for 28 of 81 adaptive profiles, versus 2 of 81 resistant profiles.
Retraining is tagged for 34 of 81 early-stage profiles, versus 11 of 81 late-stage profiles.
Collective action is tagged for 48 progressive profiles, versus 0 centre and 2 traditional profiles (81 each).

quotes.name: Elena Moreau
